{{nihongo|'''Yamanashioka Shrine, Yamanashi'''|山梨岡神社 (山梨市)}} is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|Q845945|qid=Q845945}} in {{ill|Yamanashi (city)|ar|ياماناشي (ياماناشي)|azb|یاماناشی، یاماناشی|be|Яманасі (горад)|ca|Yamanashi|ce|Яманаси (гӀала)|ceb|Yamanashi-shi|cs|Jamanaši (Jamanaši)|de|Yamanashi|es|Yamanashi|et|Yamanashi|fa|یاماناشی، یاماناشی|fi|Yamanashi|fr|Yamanashi|gl|Yamanashi|hy|Յամանասի (քաղաք)|it|Yamanashi|ja|山梨市|ko|야마나시시|mzn|یاماناشی، یاماناشی|nl|Yamanashi (stad)|pl|Yamanashi|pt|Yamanashi (cidade)|ro|Yamanashi|ru|Яманаси (город)|sv|Yamanashi|tg|Яманаши|th|ยามานาชิ (เมือง)|tl|Yamanashi, Yamanashi|tr|Yamanashi (şehir)|tt|Яманаси (шәһәр)|uk|Яманасі (Яманасі)|ur|یماناشی، یماناشی|vi|Yamanashi (thành phố)|war|Yamanashi, Yamanashi|zh|山梨市|zh_classical|山梨市|zh_min_nan|Yamanasi-chhī|zh_yue|山梨市|qid=Q840610}}, {{ill|Yamanashi Prefecture|Q132720|qid=Q132720}}. It is a former {{ill|Gō-sha|Q134917316|qid=Q134917316|lt=gōsha|qid=Q134917316}} that claims identification with the {{ill|Shikinaisha|lt=Shikinaisha|qid=Q134917286}} "Yamanashioka Shrine"<ref>However, the common scholarly view identifies the Shikinaisha "Yamanashioka Shrine" with the shrine of the same name in {{ill|Fuefuki|ar|فويفوكي (ياماناشي)|azb|فوئه‌فوکی، یاماناشی|ca|Fuefuki|ce|Фуэфуки|ceb|Fuefuki-shi|de|Fuefuki|es|Fuefuki|fa|فوئه‌فوکی، یاماناشی|fi|Fuefuki|fr|Fuefuki|gl|Fuefuki|hy|Ֆուեֆուկի|it|Fuefuki|ja|笛吹市|ko|후에후키시|mzn|فوئه‌فوکی، یاماناشی|nl|Fuefuki|pl|Fuefuki|pt|Fuefuki|ro|Fuefuki|ru|Фуэфуки|sv|Fuefuki|tg|Фуефуки|th|ฟูเอฟูกิ|tl|Fuefuki|tr|Fuefuki|tt|Фуэфуки|tum|Fuefuki|uk|Фуефукі (Яманасі)|ur|فیو فوکی|vi|Fuefuki, Yamanashi|war|Fuefuki, Yamanashi|zh|笛吹市|zh_classical|笛吹市|zh_min_nan|Huehuki-chhī|zh_yue|笛吹|qid=Q849434}}, a former gōsha.</ref>. {{nihongo|'''Yamanashioka Shrine, Yamanashi'''|山梨岡神社 (山梨市)}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Kai Province]].

The shrine stands on a small hill in flat land known as "Ishimori-yama" or "Ishimori-oka"<ref>There is a tradition that {{ill|Daidarabotchi|de|Daidarabotchi|es|Daidarabotchi|id|Daidarabotchi|it|Daidarabotchi|ja|ダイダラボッチ|ko|다이다라봇치|ms|Daidarabotchi|pt|Daidara-bocchi|ro|Daidarabotchi|zh|大太法師|qid=Q1157529}} built it.</ref>. Though compact, the precinct has large trees such as pines and many strange rocks, and is known as a famous spot for {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=azaleas}}. It was long loved by men of letters, and individual rocks were given distinctive names<ref>It is also pointed out that most of these rocks were once largely buried and only slightly exposed, so it is uncertain whether the site was called "Yamanashioka" at the time of the '{{ill|Engishiki|Q1342448|qid=Q1342448}}' compilation or earlier ("Survey Report").</ref>.

== Shrine name ==
A folk etymology says the area, being lacking in relief, was called "yama-nashi" (no mountain), which later became "Yamanashi"<ref>"Jinja Meisaichō," quoted in "Survey Report."</ref>. In addition, the '{{ill|Kaikokushi|Q11577871|qid=Q11577871}}' of {{ill|Bunka|Q1373146|qid=Q1373146|lt=Bunka}} 11 ({{ill|1814|Q6943|qid=Q6943}}) records the then shrine name as "Kumano Gongen."

== Enshrined deities ==
It enshrines six {{ill|pillars|Q16283888|qid=Q16283888|lt=pillars}}: {{ill|Izanami|lt=Izanami-no-Mikoto|qid=Q682306}}, {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Kotosakanoo-no-Mikoto}}, {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Hayatamao-no-Mikoto}}, {{ill|Kuni-no-Tokotachi|ca|Kunitokotatchi|es|Kunitokotachi|fr|Kunitokotachi|it|Kuni-no-Tokotachi|ja|国之常立神|mni|ꯀꯨꯅꯤ-ꯅꯣ-ꯇꯣꯀꯣꯇꯆꯤ|ru|Куни-но токотати-но микото|simple|Kuni-no-Tokotachi|th|คูนิ โนะ โทโกตาจิ|uk|Куні но токотаті но камі|zh|國常立尊|qid=Q478504|lt=Kunitokotachi-no-Mikoto}}, {{ill|Ōkuninushi|lt=Ōkuninushi-no-Mikoto|qid=Q276944}}, and {{ill|Sukunabikona|lt=Sukunahikona-no-Mikoto|qid=Q3275687}}.

The '{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Kai Meishōshi}}' and '{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Kai Kokushi}}' of {{ill|Tenmei|Q1194121|qid=Q1194121}} 7 ({{ill|1787|Q7763|qid=Q7763}}) say the shrine jointly enshrined {{ill|Kumano Gongen|Q11568925|qid=Q11568925}} and '''Kunitachi Myōjin'''; the first three deities above correspond to the former, and the latter three to the latter.

== Origin tradition ==
According to shrine tradition, the original founding year is unknown, but it is said {{ill|Yamato Takeru|lt=Yamato Takeru|qid=Q461258}} invited the deity during his expedition against the eastern peoples, and one tradition says it was founded by Yamato Takeru in {{ill|Emperor Keikō|Q329723|qid=Q329723}} 41 ({{ill|AD 111|Q30640|qid=Q30640}})<ref name="平凡社">'Shintō Daijiten.'</ref>. East of the honden is the '''Mikoshikake-ishi''', said to be the stone where Yamato Takeru sat. It is further said that in {{ill|Jingo-keiun|Q1373049|qid=Q1373049}} 2 ({{ill|768|Q29961|qid=Q29961}}), {{ill|Sakanoue no Karitamaro|Q3137722|qid=Q3137722|lt=Sakanoue no Karitamaro}} built shrine buildings; later military figures also rebuilt them repeatedly, including {{ill|Kagami Tōmitsu|Q11399726|qid=Q11399726}} in {{ill|Bunji (era)|Q1194415|qid=Q1194415}} 3 ({{ill|1187|Q19731|qid=Q19731}})<ref name="平凡社"/>. In earlier times, a yearly archery rite was also held<ref>'Jinja Meikan.'</ref>.

In the {{ill|Edo period|Q184963|qid=Q184963}}, it held over 2 {{ill|Koku|Q855048|qid=Q855048}} 5 {{ill|To (unit)|Q1078168|qid=Q1078168}} of shuinchi and over 3 koku 7 to of kokuinchi, and in {{ill|Meiji era|ar|فترة مييجي|ast|Dómina Meiji|az|Meydzi dövrü|azb|مئی‌جی دؤورو|be|Перыяд Мэйдзі|bn|মেইজি যুগ|bo|མེའི་ཇིའི་དུས་དུས་མཚམས།|ca|Era Meiji|cs|Období Meidži|da|Meiji-perioden|de|Meiji-Zeit|el|Μεϊτζί (περίοδος)|es|Era Meiji|et|Meiji periood|eu|Meiji Aroa|fa|دوره میجی|fi|Meiji-kausi|fr|Ère Meiji|gl|Período Meiji|he|תקופת מייג'י|hr|Meiji (razdoblje)|ht|Epòk Meiji|hu|Meidzsi-kor|id|Zaman Meiji|io|Ero Meiji|is|Meiji-tímabilið|it|Periodo Meiji|ja|明治|ka|მეიძის ეპოქა|kbp|Mejii wɛɛ yaa alɩwaatʊ|kk|Мэйдзи дәуірі|ko|메이지 시대|la|Aetas Meiji|lt|Meidži laikotarpis|lv|Meidzi periods|mk|Меиџи (период)|mn|Мэйжийн эрин|ms|Zaman Meiji|nl|Meijiperiode|nn|Meiji|no|Meiji-perioden|pl|Meiji (okres)|pt|Era Meiji|ro|Perioada Meiji|ru|Мэйдзи|simple|Meiji period|sk|Obdobie Meidži|sq|Periudha Meixhi|sr|Меиџи период|sv|Meijiperioden|ta|மெய்சி காலம்|th|ยุคเมจิ|tl|Panahong Meiji|tr|Meiji Dönemi|uk|Період Мейдзі|ur|میجی دور|vi|Thời kỳ Minh Trị|war|Panahon Meiji|wuu|明治|zh|明治|zh_classical|明治|zh_min_nan|Bêng-tī|zh_yue|明治|qid=Q3125096}} 6 ({{ill|1873|Q7757|qid=Q7757}}) it was ranked gōsha.

== Subordinate shrines ==
* Tenjin-sha - enshrines Yamato Takeru; stands on top of the above Mikoshikake-ishi.

== Shrine architecture ==
The honden is a two-seat {{ill|Aidono|Q135009883|qid=Q135009883}} niken-sha {{ill|Nagare-zukuri|Q210684|qid=Q210684}} with copper-plate roofing. The {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=moya}} has gable-side ornamentation such as {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=gegyo}} and board-style {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=kaerumata}}; the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=tokyō}} are demi-bracket sets with {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=kobushi-bana}}; it has an engawa with {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=giboshi}} railings, and rear side panels are {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=waki-shōji}}. The one-bay {{ill|kōhai|Q11415970|qid=Q11415970}} uses chamfered square posts and is connected to the moya by an "ebi" {{ill|kōryō|Q124421222|qid=Q124421222}} beam. Decorative details preserve {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Momoyama-period}} techniques. It was designated a Yamanashi Prefecture {{ill|Tangible Cultural Property (Japan)|Q2901860|qid=Q2901860}} on November 7, {{ill|1960|Q3754|qid=Q3754}} ({{ill|Shōwa era|Q327567|qid=Q327567}} 35). In dismantling repairs the next year (1961), ink writing found behind a {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=daito}} indicated repair in {{ill|Genroku|Q1325001|qid=Q1325001}} 16 ({{ill|1703|Q6822|qid=Q6822}}), making it a valuable dated structure<ref>'Yamanashi Prefectural History: Cultural Properties Volume,' Yamanashi Prefecture, 1999.</ref>.
